claims.text: The baseline consists of zirconium-alloy cladding with a conventional elemental Cr coating applied by sputtering.
Elemental Cr coatings can fail because of significant Cr–Zr interdiffusion, particularly during high-temperature steam exposure.
Reactive magnetron sputtering in an N2-containing atmosphere can produce a Cr/CrN nanolaminate coating.
The proposed deposition process will place an ultrathin CrN layer at the interface between the Cr topcoat and zirconium-alloy substrate.
Process optimization, in situ monitoring, and post-deposition characterization can ensure that the CrN barrier is continuous, uniform, and defect-free.
An interfacial continuous ultrathin CrN layer acts as a physical barrier to Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
An interfacial continuous ultrathin CrN layer acts as a chemical barrier to Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
CrN is chemically stable under the proposed exposure conditions.
CrN has a high melting temperature relevant to the proposed high-temperature application.
CrN has sufficiently low diffusivity to impede Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will reduce degradation of the Cr coating during high-temperature and prolonged oxidizing exposures.
The Cr/CrN coating will show less interfacial Cr–Zr transport than an unmodified elemental Cr coating.
The Cr/CrN coating will have better oxidation resistance than an unmodified elemental Cr coating.
The Cr/CrN coating will retain better mechanical integrity than an unmodified elemental Cr coating.
The predicted benefits apply during steam exposure at temperatures up to 1200°C for up to 1 hour.
The predicted benefits apply during subcritical-water exposure at approximately 280°C for up to 3000 hours.
Defects or nonuniformity in the CrN barrier may reduce its effectiveness.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance, coating integrity, and suppression of Cr–Zr interdiffusion relative to the elemental-Cr control would falsify the hypothesis.
